medical.title: Thousands of new mothers across Britain suffering from undiagnosed PTSD after childbirth, study suggests
medical.summary: Tens of thousands of new mothers across Britain may be suffering from undiagnosed PTSD following childbirth, according to a University of East Anglia report.

medical.title: Pre-cancerous blood cells may fuel disease risk by prematurely aging the bone marrow
medical.summary: Precancerous blood cells can actively reshape their surroundings, prematurely aging cells in the bone marrow to create conditions that favor their own growth and potentially increase the risk of blood cancer, according to a new study by researchers at The Jackson Laboratory (JAX).

medical.title: Heart failure drugs may work within days by boosting cells' energy supply
medical.summary: Researchers have discovered that SGLT2 inhibitors, a class of drugs originally developed to treat diabetes and now widely used for heart failure, work by activating a key enzyme that helps heart cells produce and use energy more efficiently. The study, published today in Science, potentially solves a longstanding gap in knowledge about these drugs and opens the door to potential new treatments for heart failure.

medical.title: Researchers develop scalable method to generate key immune cells for cancer therapy
medical.summary: Researchers at the Center for Regenerative Medicine (CReM) at Boston Medical Center (BMC) and Boston University (BU) have developed a scalable method for generating CD4+ helper T cells from induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), overcoming a longstanding challenge in the development of stem cell-based immunotherapies. The findings, published in Stem Cell Reports, could help advance efforts to create off-the-shelf CAR-T cell therapies that can be produced at scale and made more readily available to patients.

medical.title: Cell therapy substantially reduces severe rheumatoid arthritis in first clinical trial
medical.summary: Immunotherapies such as CAR T-cell therapy are used primarily to treat cancer. In the future, these patient-specific therapies, manufactured from patients' own immune cells, could also help cure autoimmune diseases. Six patients with particularly severe rheumatoid arthritis have now received this treatment at Charité—Universitätsmedizin Berlin. In the journal Nature Medicine, the researchers report the results from the world's first clinical trial of its kind: Disease activity decreased substantially in all participants. By the end of the observation period, three of the patients no longer required any medication for rheumatoid arthritis.

medical.title: South Africa sounds alarm as infant vaccinations plummet
medical.summary: South Africa's infant vaccination rate has fallen to its lowest level in years, with more than a third of babies receiving no vaccines at the start of 2026, the health department said Thursday.

medical.title: Chess as a therapeutic tool: Two studies show potential for improved quality of life
medical.summary: For several years, researchers at the Central Institute of Mental Health (CIMH) have been investigating whether chess-based cognitive training can also have therapeutic benefits. Two recent studies involving people with alcohol dependence, as well as children and adolescents with mental health conditions, now show that such training can improve quality of life and enhance cognitive abilities.

medical.title: Injectable microgels for targeted keloid radiotherapy
medical.summary: Keloids are abnormal fibroproliferative scars that form when overactive fibroblasts produce excessive collagen after skin injury. Unlike ordinary scars, they can extend beyond the original wound and cause itching, pain and tenderness.

medical.title: Practice helps the brain separate tasks and improve multitasking ability
medical.summary: It is commonly perceived that multitasking is highly inefficient, with the brain often "crashing" or scrambling when trying to do two things at once. A recent study by City University of Hong Kong (CityUHK) has uncovered the mechanism behind this, revealing how the brain dynamically reorganizes itself to break through this cognitive bottleneck and achieve efficient, simultaneous multitasking.

medical.title: Parkinson's an unexpected and unpredictable journey for Pacific Peoples
medical.summary: For Pacific Peoples, being diagnosed with Parkinson's is like being in a va'a/vaka on an unpredictable wave on the high seas, a University of Otago – Ōtākou Whakaihu Waka study has found.

medical.title: Current shingles vaccine linked to lower risk of coronary heart disease, stroke and heart failure
medical.summary: Shingles is a painful and serious condition affecting many older people. It is caused by the herpes zoster virus, which can flare up in people who previously had chickenpox. A vaccine against shingles (Zostavax) was introduced in 2006. In many countries, including the U.K. and U.S., Zostavax has now been withdrawn and replaced by a much more effective recombinant vaccine (Shingrix). In the U.K., Shingrix is being offered by the NHS to all older people and certain other groups.

medical.title: An 'undruggable' cancer target meets an RNA-based strategy to curb tumor growth
medical.summary: Researchers at Umeå University have developed a strategy to slow the growth of tumor cells. By targeting the genetic instructions that control the production of a key cancer-related protein, they were able to inhibit tumor cell growth. The findings are published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

medical.title: Considerable global disparities found in access to dermatological care
medical.summary: Global access to dermatological care varies significantly, with 42% of countries reporting inadequate or extremely poor access, according to a study published online Aug. 26 in JAMA Dermatology.

medical.title: Most adults with moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis may be ineligible for randomized controlled trials
medical.summary: More than half of real-world adult patients with moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis (UC) are ineligible for current randomized controlled trials (RCTs), according to a study published online Aug. 4 in Crohn's & Colitis 360.

medical.title: Unexpected discovery reveals mechanism behind brain tumor development
medical.summary: When researchers at Lund University investigated how UM171, a molecule used to make blood stem cells multiply, works, they made an unexpected connection. The results provide new insights into how one of the most common malignant brain tumors in children could be treated in the future. Their research is published in the journal Cancer Gene Therapy.

medical.title: AI model predicts indwelling catheter conversion in early neurogenic bladder
medical.summary: A novel prognostic stratification model can predict indwelling catheter conversion (ICC) among patients with early-stage spinal cord injury (SCI) and neurogenic bladder (NB), according to a study published online Aug. 23 in Neurourology and Urodynamics.

medical.title: Brain activity patterns may 'tag' experiences for later memory-making during sleep
medical.summary: The brain may "tag" experiences during learning to better consolidate memories of them during sleep, according to a study published Aug. 27 in the journal PLOS Biology by Dan Denis from the University of York, United Kingdom, and colleagues.

medical.title: Folic acid does not elevate formaldehyde in mice and humans
medical.summary: Folic acid—an essential vitamin added to flour and cereals and prescribed at high doses for cancer patients and people with blood disorders—does not elevate toxic formaldehyde in the body, according to a new study of mice and human cancer patients who consumed high doses.

medical.title: Registry-based model predicts hip fracture risk better than current screening
medical.summary: A machine-learning tool built from Swedish national health registry data can predict hip fracture risk with high accuracy without an in-person assessment and identifies far more at-risk individuals than current clinical screening practices, according to a study published Aug. 27 in the journal PLOS Medicine by Kristian Axelsson and Mattias Lorentzon of the University of Gothenburg, Sweden, and colleagues.

medical.title: Next-generation RNA approach provides hope for genetic diseases missed by current drugs
medical.summary: Researchers at the University of Toronto have developed a next-generation RNA therapeutic approach with the potential to treat a wide range of genetic diseases that share certain disease-causing mutations. The work advances an emerging platform in genetic medicine centered on transfer RNA, or tRNA. The team engineered tRNA to help cells read through premature stop signals and complete production of full-length proteins that would otherwise be truncated or absent.

medical.title: Largest ever molecular map of autism opens new paths to precision therapies
medical.summary: For more than two decades, researchers have identified hundreds of genes that increase the risk of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Yet multiple fundamental questions have remained unanswered: Among them, how do mutations in these genes lead directly to changes in brain development, and how can that knowledge be translated into more effective therapies?

medical.title: Students find AI isn't a cure all for drug discovery
medical.summary: There's been a lot of talk about artificial intelligence's potential to transform drug research and discovery—and companies are spending billions in pursuit of that dream.

medical.title: Chronic pain is reflected in the folds and grooves of the cerebral cortex
medical.summary: Persistent pain often has no clear cause. However, studies show measurable differences in the structure and activity of the brains of those affected. This might explain why they experience chronic pain. "Many of our study participants were grateful that someone was taking their symptoms seriously and conducting research into them," says neuroscientist Salome Häuselmann.

medical.title: Swimming in rivers and lakes linked to higher risk of stomach bugs and rashes
medical.summary: People swimming in rivers and lakes could be putting themselves at risk of nasty skin conditions and stomach bugs, according to a new study from the University of East Anglia. The researchers found that people who swam in rivers and lakes were more than twice as likely to develop skin problems, while higher levels of bacteria linked to fecal pollution were associated with an increased risk of stomach bugs.

medical.title: Tailoring the 'caffeine nap' to help drivers with obstructive sleep apnea manage tiredness behind the wheel
medical.summary: Researchers have issued tailored advice for drivers with obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) after finding that common guidance for tackling tiredness behind the wheel may not be the most effective approach for people with the condition.

science.title: Tiny oxygen gaps may determine whether next-generation memory films store data well
science.summary: Researchers have captured in real time the "birth moment" when the performance of a next-generation memory material is determined. The key lies in controlling oxygen vacancies, microscopic defects created when oxygen atoms are missing from their normal positions.

science.title: Boosting soybean protein: Zinc and sulfur essential in sustainable crop production
science.summary: Soybean is a critical element of the global food supply: Between its use for animal feed and human consumption, it accounts for roughly two-thirds of plant-based protein meal output worldwide. Canada is a global leader in sustainable soybean production, with 70% of its crop, one of the country's top three by value, exported annually.

science.title: Vehicle-mounted spectroscopy system detects methane in real time
science.summary: Researchers have developed a vehicle-mounted spectroscopy system that can reliably detect methane in real time while driving. Using a moving vehicle to detect methane could make it easier to locate hidden methane emissions across large areas.

science.title: Specific cover crops may help attract insects that target harmful pests
science.summary: Different cover crops may affect how plants defend themselves against pests—including by attracting more insects that eat harmful caterpillars—according to a new study led by researchers at Penn State's College of Agricultural Sciences.

science.title: Discovery reveals rapid pathways to complex aromatic molecules in space
science.summary: A team of researchers led by the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa Department of Chemistry has uncovered a faster way large carbon-based molecules may form in space, helping solve a long-standing mystery about how some of the building blocks of the universe grow.

science.title: Molecular makeover brightens organic light near 1,000 nanometers
science.summary: Near-infrared organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs) that emit about 1,000 nanometers could support biomedical and security technologies. Yet pushing organic light to these longer wavelengths usually causes a steep drop in efficiency. As the energy gap becomes smaller, molecular vibrations more readily turn excited-state energy into heat rather than light.

science.title: AI model designs potentially stable protein sequences beyond those found in nature
science.summary: A protein's function is determined by its structure, and structure—the way a protein folds—is determined by its sequence of amino acids, the building blocks of proteins.

science.title: Shear flow in narrow channels sparks amyloid formation, experiments reveal
science.summary: Many cars and not enough lanes is a recipe for traffic jams. Now, researchers from Japan show that even proteins can get backed up and start behaving poorly when too many try to squeeze too quickly through a small space.

science.title: MOF-coated catalyst converts CO₂ to CO nearly five times faster under ultrasonic vibration
science.summary: Researchers at the University of Osaka have developed a catalyst that uses mechanical vibration to convert carbon dioxide (CO2) into carbon monoxide (CO), an important chemical feedstock. The catalyst consists of barium titanate (BaTiO3) coated with a metal-organic framework (MOF)—a porous material that captures and concentrates CO2 near the catalyst surface—and incorporates isolated copper (Cu) atoms as reaction sites.

science.title: Texas fossil reveals early insects kept aquatic limbs during move onto land
science.summary: The formation of complex terrestrial ecosystems was a significant innovation in the evolutionary history of life on Earth. This event signified the expansion of life beyond marine environments and marked the beginning of a new phase in the diversification of terrestrial biota.

science.title: Groundbreaking literacy program triples rate of progress among struggling young readers
science.summary: A University of Alberta literacy expert has completed the largest reading intervention in Canadian history, tripling the rate of progress for most participants after just five months. Preliminary results show that about half of the children in the program require no further intervention.

science.title: ASTRID traces 13.5 billion years of black hole and galaxy evolution
science.summary: In dark skies at night, distant starlight twinkles and speaks to vast cosmic histories almost as old as time itself. New data from instruments such as NASA's James Webb Space Telescope are helping astrophysicists probe deep cosmic mysteries, including the evolution of black holes and galaxies.

science.title: Milky Way's own gravity can mimic dark matter clues, stellar stream simulations suggest
science.summary: Most of the stars in our Milky Way galaxy sit neatly on a flat plane. But the space around our galaxy is much more chaotic. Rogue bands of stars called "stellar streams" orbit the Milky Way much like planets in our solar system orbit the sun.

science.title: Fast but error-prone AI assists in solving a decades-old fluid mechanics problem in five weeks
science.summary: An AI assistant helped University of Colorado Boulder researchers solve a mathematical problem that had challenged their lab for a year and a half, though it made subtle errors along the way. The breakthrough could improve how scientists study nanoparticles—tiny particles about 1,000 times thinner than a human hair—but it reveals both the promise and limitations of AI as a scientific research partner.

science.title: Social media posts reveal how communities cope with extreme heat
science.summary: As extreme heat becomes more frequent and intense across California, knowing which communities are struggling and what kind of help they need is increasingly important for protecting public health. A new UC Irvine study suggests that part of the answer may be hiding in everyday conversations on social media.

science.title: Parental care can influence evolution, beetle experiments show
science.summary: How has offspring dependence on parents evolved over the course of evolution? Researchers at the University of Bayreuth, in collaboration with Kyoto University, Japan, have investigated one possible mechanism by studying the burying beetle Nicrophorus vespilloides. Their new study shows that parents do more than simply provide care for their offspring: They also improve the entire developmental environment in which their young grow up, a factor that may itself have influenced evolutionary change. The findings have been published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

science.title: How bacteria develop resistance to programmable antibiotics
science.summary: Antimicrobial resistance is one of the greatest challenges facing modern medicine. A new class of programmable antibiotics known as asobiotics can be used to treat bacterial infections when classical antibiotics fail. A team of researchers from TWINCORE, Center for Experimental and Clinical Infection Research; the RESIST Cluster of Excellence; and the Helmholtz Institute for RNA-based Infection Research (HIRI) in Würzburg has now studied how bacteria adapt to asobiotics. They recently published their findings in Nature Communications.

science.title: Mirror-image molecules steer electron spins and lift perovskite solar cell efficiency
science.summary: Some molecules come in two "handed" forms. This property, called chirality, can influence not only how molecules interact with light but also which electron spins they allow to pass. Researchers at the University of Osaka have developed novel chiral hole-transport materials that shed new light on this unusual effect while also improving the interfaces of perovskite solar cells.

science.title: Study on biodiversity conservation in agriculture and forestry: High motivation, few options
science.summary: Farmers and foresters manage around 80% of Germany's land area. They are therefore key agents of change in protecting biodiversity—and are often accused of not doing enough to protect it.

science.title: Researchers reveal the unique 'tagging' mechanism that guides the sleeping brain in remembering key thoughts
science.summary: Why do we remember certain moments while forgetting others? Every day, our minds are bombarded with thousands of pieces of information, yet our brains have a limited capacity to consolidate these experiences into lasting memories. This means we need a way to hold on to what is most important and disregard irrelevant details.

science.title: JWST finds early galaxies may be 4 times more massive than thought
science.summary: Astronomers using JWST have discovered that massive early galaxies contain far more small, faint stars than expected. That hidden population could make some of these galaxies three to four times more massive than previous estimates. The finding makes it even harder to explain how enormous, mature galaxies formed so soon after the Big Bang. It could also suggest that planets around low-mass stars were more common in the early universe than scientists realized.

science.title: Archaeologists discover mysterious 400-year-old Indigenous pot in Florida
science.summary: A tiny, fully intact Indigenous pot buried for roughly 400 years has left archaeologists wondering why such a usable object was deliberately abandoned. Found at a historic Potano-Timucua village in Florida, the mysterious vessel is helping reveal a complex world of Native traditions, Spanish influence, trade, and migration.

environment.title: Costa Rica to require wildlife crossings for roads when they impact fauna
environment.summary: Costa Rican lawmakers unanimously voted to require wildlife crossings for new and existing road infrastructure when evidence shows the infrastructure interrupts natural connectivity and threatens wildlife safety. The measure, approved in August 2026, will help wildlife avoid being struck by cars while crossing roads and connect habitat, the regulation notes. Once signed into law by […]

environment.title: Australia’s 30×30 conservation promise matters a lot, but how it’s achieved is key (commentary)
environment.summary: Australia has just four years to meet a global biodiversity promise: Protect 30% of its land and seas by 2030. What happens here in one of the planet’s megadiverse nations, which is also an extinction hotspot, will signal whether the world’s most ambitious conservation commitment can succeed. Australia is a wealthy country with abundant resources, […]

environment.title: More than 380 coastal World Heritage Sites may face climate risks, new data shows
environment.summary: Whenever coastal engineer Robert Nicholls looks outside one of his home’s windows, he can see the Hurst Castle Spit on the south coast of England slowly eroding across the sea. “In a way, Hurst Castle is a part of me, because I did all my Ph.D. work on the spit.” ​Although this particular castle doesn’t […]

environment.title: US environmental groups plan to sue to relist gray whales under Endangered Species Act
environment.summary: A group of environmental organizations announced their intent to sue the United States National Marine Fisheries Services (NMFS) for failing to consider protections for Eastern Pacific gray whales under the Endangered Species Act (ESA). Gray whales (Eschrichtius robustus) are experiencing a potentially catastrophic population decline, a sharp reversal from what had been considered a conservation […]

environment.title: 3,500-year-old skeletons challenge what scientists thought they knew about syphilis
environment.summary: Ancient remains from Vietnam suggest diseases like yaws may have been passed from mother to child thousands of years ago, a form of transmission often assumed to indicate syphilis. The discovery could overturn how scientists interpret ancient infections and complicate the long-running mystery of syphilis’s origins.

environment.title: Scientists find evidence for two origins of life on Earth
environment.summary: Scientists probing life’s deepest origins have uncovered evidence that the first free-living cells may have emerged not once, but twice. The findings suggest a striking possibility: life may share one ancient genetic code, yet have undergone two separate transitions into free-living existence.

environment.title: “Cannot be explained” – New super steel stuns scientists
environment.summary: Scientists have created an unusually corrosion-resistant stainless steel that could replace costly titanium components used to produce green hydrogen. The breakthrough could reduce structural material costs by roughly 40 times and make seawater-based hydrogen production far more economical.

environment.title: King Harold may have lost England by backing the wrong pope
environment.summary: A forgotten fragment of a lost papal letter is offering a surprising new explanation for the Norman Conquest. England may have backed the wrong pope during a bitter religious power struggle, giving Pope Alexander II a political reason to support William the Conqueror’s invasion. The discovery suggests Harold’s downfall in 1066 was shaped by intrigue in Rome as well as bloodshed at Hastings.

environment.title: 150-million-year-old dinosaur footprints reveal something strange about its walk
environment.summary: A spectacular 150-million-year-old trail of more than 130 footprints captures a giant sauropod making a complete loop before continuing on its way. Its uneven stride hints that the long-necked dinosaur may have been walking with a limp.

environment.title: The secret hidden in these ancient manuscripts isn’t written in ink
environment.summary: Researchers can now recover DNA from centuries-old parchment without damaging the manuscripts, turning historic documents into unexpected genetic time capsules. The hidden clues could reveal ancient trade routes, livestock history, manuscript origins, and details of everyday life stretching back more than a thousand years.

environment.title: Earth’s molten core suddenly reversed direction — and scientists don’t know why
environment.summary: Earth’s molten iron core unexpectedly reversed direction beneath the Pacific, revealing a dramatic change in the hidden engine that creates our planet’s magnetic field. Satellite data suggest the surge is already weakening, raising the possibility that the deep-Earth upheaval is part of a mysterious natural cycle.

environment.title: Scientists find unexpected life on Ötzi the Iceman’s 5,300-year-old body
environment.summary: More than 5,000 years after his death, Ötzi the Iceman is still hosting a remarkable mix of ancient and modern microorganisms. Researchers separated microbes that lived in his body during his lifetime from those that arrived after his death, uncovering traces of his original gut bacteria and cold-loving yeasts that may have survived alongside him in the glacier for millennia.

environment.title: Scientists rediscover lost Megalodon fossils—and reveal a 79-foot giant
environment.summary: Several enormous Megalodon vertebrae thought to have been destroyed in 1989 were found sitting unnoticed on a museum shelf. Their analysis strengthens evidence that the giant shark could exceed 24 meters (79 feet) in length and live for nearly a century. Researchers also estimate that its newborns may have measured an astonishing 3.6 meters (12 feet).

mix_items.summary: Compania Naţională de Investiţii Rutiere (CNIR) a stabilit împărţirea Autostrăzii A13 Braşov - Bacău, cu o lungime de 174 de kilometri, în cinci loturi, fiecare dintre acestea urmând să poată funcţiona independent.

mix_items.summary: Secretarul de stat în Ministerul Transporturilor şi Infrastructurii (MTI), Horaţiu Cosma, a anunţat, joi, că au fost avizate în Consiliul Interministerial de avizare a investiţiilor publice patru proiecte esenţiale pentru infrastructura rutieră a României, dintre care două reprezintă autostrăzi. mix_items.title: Tiny oxygen gaps may determine whether next-generation memory films store data well
mix_items.summary: Researchers have captured in real time the "birth moment" when the performance of a next-generation memory material is determined. The key lies in controlling oxygen vacancies, microscopic defects created when oxygen atoms are missing from their normal positions.

mix_items.summary: București, 17 iulie 2026 – Teach for Romania a dat startul Academiei de Leadership și Formare în Educație, programul intensiv prin care pregătește cea de-a 13-a generație de viitori lideri în educație – directori, profesori, învățători și educatori, care să predea, începând cu anul școlar 2026-2027, și să transforme educația de la firul ierbii, în […]

mix_items.summary: Asociația The Da Vinci System (Cluj) - Educație pentru siguranța copiilor în mediul online. Articolul WEBTECTIVII apare prima dată în World Vision România .

mix_items.summary: Tens of thousands of new mothers across Britain may be suffering from undiagnosed PTSD following childbirth, according to a University of East Anglia report.

mix_items.title: Boosting soybean protein: Zinc and sulfur essential in sustainable crop production
mix_items.summary: Soybean is a critical element of the global food supply: Between its use for animal feed and human consumption, it accounts for roughly two-thirds of plant-based protein meal output worldwide. Canada is a global leader in sustainable soybean production, with 70% of its crop, one of the country's top three by value, exported annually.

mix_items.title: Vehicle-mounted spectroscopy system detects methane in real time
mix_items.summary: Researchers have developed a vehicle-mounted spectroscopy system that can reliably detect methane in real time while driving. Using a moving vehicle to detect methane could make it easier to locate hidden methane emissions across large areas.

mix_items.title: Specific cover crops may help attract insects that target harmful pests
mix_items.summary: Different cover crops may affect how plants defend themselves against pests—including by attracting more insects that eat harmful caterpillars—according to a new study led by researchers at Penn State's College of Agricultural Sciences.

mix_items.title: Discovery reveals rapid pathways to complex aromatic molecules in space
mix_items.summary: A team of researchers led by the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa Department of Chemistry has uncovered a faster way large carbon-based molecules may form in space, helping solve a long-standing mystery about how some of the building blocks of the universe grow.

mix_items.title: Molecular makeover brightens organic light near 1,000 nanometers
mix_items.summary: Near-infrared organic light-emitting diodes (OLEDs) that emit about 1,000 nanometers could support biomedical and security technologies. Yet pushing organic light to these longer wavelengths usually causes a steep drop in efficiency. As the energy gap becomes smaller, molecular vibrations more readily turn excited-state energy into heat rather than light.

mix_items.title: AI model designs potentially stable protein sequences beyond those found in nature
mix_items.summary: A protein's function is determined by its structure, and structure—the way a protein folds—is determined by its sequence of amino acids, the building blocks of proteins.

mix_items.title: Shear flow in narrow channels sparks amyloid formation, experiments reveal
mix_items.summary: Many cars and not enough lanes is a recipe for traffic jams. Now, researchers from Japan show that even proteins can get backed up and start behaving poorly when too many try to squeeze too quickly through a small space.

mix_items.title: MOF-coated catalyst converts CO₂ to CO nearly five times faster under ultrasonic vibration
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the University of Osaka have developed a catalyst that uses mechanical vibration to convert carbon dioxide (CO2) into carbon monoxide (CO), an important chemical feedstock. The catalyst consists of barium titanate (BaTiO3) coated with a metal-organic framework (MOF)—a porous material that captures and concentrates CO2 near the catalyst surface—and incorporates isolated copper (Cu) atoms as reaction sites.

mix_items.title: Pre-cancerous blood cells may fuel disease risk by prematurely aging the bone marrow
mix_items.summary: Precancerous blood cells can actively reshape their surroundings, prematurely aging cells in the bone marrow to create conditions that favor their own growth and potentially increase the risk of blood cancer, according to a new study by researchers at The Jackson Laboratory (JAX).

mix_items.title: Heart failure drugs may work within days by boosting cells' energy supply
mix_items.summary: Researchers have discovered that SGLT2 inhibitors, a class of drugs originally developed to treat diabetes and now widely used for heart failure, work by activating a key enzyme that helps heart cells produce and use energy more efficiently. The study, published today in Science, potentially solves a longstanding gap in knowledge about these drugs and opens the door to potential new treatments for heart failure.

mix_items.title: Texas fossil reveals early insects kept aquatic limbs during move onto land
mix_items.summary: The formation of complex terrestrial ecosystems was a significant innovation in the evolutionary history of life on Earth. This event signified the expansion of life beyond marine environments and marked the beginning of a new phase in the diversification of terrestrial biota.

mix_items.title: Groundbreaking literacy program triples rate of progress among struggling young readers
mix_items.summary: A University of Alberta literacy expert has completed the largest reading intervention in Canadian history, tripling the rate of progress for most participants after just five months. Preliminary results show that about half of the children in the program require no further intervention.

mix_items.title: ASTRID traces 13.5 billion years of black hole and galaxy evolution
mix_items.summary: In dark skies at night, distant starlight twinkles and speaks to vast cosmic histories almost as old as time itself. New data from instruments such as NASA's James Webb Space Telescope are helping astrophysicists probe deep cosmic mysteries, including the evolution of black holes and galaxies.

mix_items.title: Costa Rica to require wildlife crossings for roads when they impact fauna
mix_items.summary: Costa Rican lawmakers unanimously voted to require wildlife crossings for new and existing road infrastructure when evidence shows the infrastructure interrupts natural connectivity and threatens wildlife safety. The measure, approved in August 2026, will help wildlife avoid being struck by cars while crossing roads and connect habitat, the regulation notes. Once signed into law by […]

mix_items.title: Researchers develop scalable method to generate key immune cells for cancer therapy
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the Center for Regenerative Medicine (CReM) at Boston Medical Center (BMC) and Boston University (BU) have developed a scalable method for generating CD4+ helper T cells from induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs), overcoming a longstanding challenge in the development of stem cell-based immunotherapies. The findings, published in Stem Cell Reports, could help advance efforts to create off-the-shelf CAR-T cell therapies that can be produced at scale and made more readily available to patients.

mix_items.title: Milky Way's own gravity can mimic dark matter clues, stellar stream simulations suggest
mix_items.summary: Most of the stars in our Milky Way galaxy sit neatly on a flat plane. But the space around our galaxy is much more chaotic. Rogue bands of stars called "stellar streams" orbit the Milky Way much like planets in our solar system orbit the sun.

mix_items.title: Fast but error-prone AI assists in solving a decades-old fluid mechanics problem in five weeks
mix_items.summary: An AI assistant helped University of Colorado Boulder researchers solve a mathematical problem that had challenged their lab for a year and a half, though it made subtle errors along the way. The breakthrough could improve how scientists study nanoparticles—tiny particles about 1,000 times thinner than a human hair—but it reveals both the promise and limitations of AI as a scientific research partner.

mix_items.title: Cell therapy substantially reduces severe rheumatoid arthritis in first clinical trial
mix_items.summary: Immunotherapies such as CAR T-cell therapy are used primarily to treat cancer. In the future, these patient-specific therapies, manufactured from patients' own immune cells, could also help cure autoimmune diseases. Six patients with particularly severe rheumatoid arthritis have now received this treatment at Charité—Universitätsmedizin Berlin. In the journal Nature Medicine, the researchers report the results from the world's first clinical trial of its kind: Disease activity decreased substantially in all participants. By the end of the observation period, three of the patients no longer required any medication for rheumatoid arthritis.

mix_items.title: South Africa sounds alarm as infant vaccinations plummet
mix_items.summary: South Africa's infant vaccination rate has fallen to its lowest level in years, with more than a third of babies receiving no vaccines at the start of 2026, the health department said Thursday.

mix_items.title: Social media posts reveal how communities cope with extreme heat
mix_items.summary: As extreme heat becomes more frequent and intense across California, knowing which communities are struggling and what kind of help they need is increasingly important for protecting public health. A new UC Irvine study suggests that part of the answer may be hiding in everyday conversations on social media.

mix_items.title: Chess as a therapeutic tool: Two studies show potential for improved quality of life
mix_items.summary: For several years, researchers at the Central Institute of Mental Health (CIMH) have been investigating whether chess-based cognitive training can also have therapeutic benefits. Two recent studies involving people with alcohol dependence, as well as children and adolescents with mental health conditions, now show that such training can improve quality of life and enhance cognitive abilities.

mix_items.title: Parental care can influence evolution, beetle experiments show
mix_items.summary: How has offspring dependence on parents evolved over the course of evolution? Researchers at the University of Bayreuth, in collaboration with Kyoto University, Japan, have investigated one possible mechanism by studying the burying beetle Nicrophorus vespilloides. Their new study shows that parents do more than simply provide care for their offspring: They also improve the entire developmental environment in which their young grow up, a factor that may itself have influenced evolutionary change. The findings have been published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

mix_items.title: Injectable microgels for targeted keloid radiotherapy
mix_items.summary: Keloids are abnormal fibroproliferative scars that form when overactive fibroblasts produce excessive collagen after skin injury. Unlike ordinary scars, they can extend beyond the original wound and cause itching, pain and tenderness.

mix_items.title: Practice helps the brain separate tasks and improve multitasking ability
mix_items.summary: It is commonly perceived that multitasking is highly inefficient, with the brain often "crashing" or scrambling when trying to do two things at once. A recent study by City University of Hong Kong (CityUHK) has uncovered the mechanism behind this, revealing how the brain dynamically reorganizes itself to break through this cognitive bottleneck and achieve efficient, simultaneous multitasking.

mix_items.title: Parkinson's an unexpected and unpredictable journey for Pacific Peoples
mix_items.summary: For Pacific Peoples, being diagnosed with Parkinson's is like being in a va'a/vaka on an unpredictable wave on the high seas, a University of Otago – Ōtākou Whakaihu Waka study has found.

mix_items.title: How bacteria develop resistance to programmable antibiotics
mix_items.summary: Antimicrobial resistance is one of the greatest challenges facing modern medicine. A new class of programmable antibiotics known as asobiotics can be used to treat bacterial infections when classical antibiotics fail. A team of researchers from TWINCORE, Center for Experimental and Clinical Infection Research; the RESIST Cluster of Excellence; and the Helmholtz Institute for RNA-based Infection Research (HIRI) in Würzburg has now studied how bacteria adapt to asobiotics. They recently published their findings in Nature Communications.

mix_items.title: Current shingles vaccine linked to lower risk of coronary heart disease, stroke and heart failure
mix_items.summary: Shingles is a painful and serious condition affecting many older people. It is caused by the herpes zoster virus, which can flare up in people who previously had chickenpox. A vaccine against shingles (Zostavax) was introduced in 2006. In many countries, including the U.K. and U.S., Zostavax has now been withdrawn and replaced by a much more effective recombinant vaccine (Shingrix). In the U.K., Shingrix is being offered by the NHS to all older people and certain other groups.

mix_items.title: An 'undruggable' cancer target meets an RNA-based strategy to curb tumor growth
mix_items.summary: Researchers at Umeå University have developed a strategy to slow the growth of tumor cells. By targeting the genetic instructions that control the production of a key cancer-related protein, they were able to inhibit tumor cell growth. The findings are published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

mix_items.title: Mirror-image molecules steer electron spins and lift perovskite solar cell efficiency
mix_items.summary: Some molecules come in two "handed" forms. This property, called chirality, can influence not only how molecules interact with light but also which electron spins they allow to pass. Researchers at the University of Osaka have developed novel chiral hole-transport materials that shed new light on this unusual effect while also improving the interfaces of perovskite solar cells.

mix_items.title: Considerable global disparities found in access to dermatological care
mix_items.summary: Global access to dermatological care varies significantly, with 42% of countries reporting inadequate or extremely poor access, according to a study published online Aug. 26 in JAMA Dermatology.

mix_items.title: Australia’s 30×30 conservation promise matters a lot, but how it’s achieved is key (commentary)
mix_items.summary: Australia has just four years to meet a global biodiversity promise: Protect 30% of its land and seas by 2030. What happens here in one of the planet’s megadiverse nations, which is also an extinction hotspot, will signal whether the world’s most ambitious conservation commitment can succeed. Australia is a wealthy country with abundant resources, […]

mix_items.title: Study on biodiversity conservation in agriculture and forestry: High motivation, few options
mix_items.summary: Farmers and foresters manage around 80% of Germany's land area. They are therefore key agents of change in protecting biodiversity—and are often accused of not doing enough to protect it.

mix_items.title: Most adults with moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis may be ineligible for randomized controlled trials
mix_items.summary: More than half of real-world adult patients with moderate-to-severe ulcerative colitis (UC) are ineligible for current randomized controlled trials (RCTs), according to a study published online Aug. 4 in Crohn's & Colitis 360.

mix_items.title: Unexpected discovery reveals mechanism behind brain tumor development
mix_items.summary: When researchers at Lund University investigated how UM171, a molecule used to make blood stem cells multiply, works, they made an unexpected connection. The results provide new insights into how one of the most common malignant brain tumors in children could be treated in the future. Their research is published in the journal Cancer Gene Therapy.

mix_items.title: AI model predicts indwelling catheter conversion in early neurogenic bladder
mix_items.summary: A novel prognostic stratification model can predict indwelling catheter conversion (ICC) among patients with early-stage spinal cord injury (SCI) and neurogenic bladder (NB), according to a study published online Aug. 23 in Neurourology and Urodynamics.

mix_items.title: More than 380 coastal World Heritage Sites may face climate risks, new data shows
mix_items.summary: Whenever coastal engineer Robert Nicholls looks outside one of his home’s windows, he can see the Hurst Castle Spit on the south coast of England slowly eroding across the sea. “In a way, Hurst Castle is a part of me, because I did all my Ph.D. work on the spit.” ​Although this particular castle doesn’t […]

mix_items.title: Researchers reveal the unique 'tagging' mechanism that guides the sleeping brain in remembering key thoughts
mix_items.summary: Why do we remember certain moments while forgetting others? Every day, our minds are bombarded with thousands of pieces of information, yet our brains have a limited capacity to consolidate these experiences into lasting memories. This means we need a way to hold on to what is most important and disregard irrelevant details.

mix_items.title: Brain activity patterns may 'tag' experiences for later memory-making during sleep
mix_items.summary: The brain may "tag" experiences during learning to better consolidate memories of them during sleep, according to a study published Aug. 27 in the journal PLOS Biology by Dan Denis from the University of York, United Kingdom, and colleagues.

mix_items.title: Folic acid does not elevate formaldehyde in mice and humans
mix_items.summary: Folic acid—an essential vitamin added to flour and cereals and prescribed at high doses for cancer patients and people with blood disorders—does not elevate toxic formaldehyde in the body, according to a new study of mice and human cancer patients who consumed high doses.

mix_items.title: Registry-based model predicts hip fracture risk better than current screening
mix_items.summary: A machine-learning tool built from Swedish national health registry data can predict hip fracture risk with high accuracy without an in-person assessment and identifies far more at-risk individuals than current clinical screening practices, according to a study published Aug. 27 in the journal PLOS Medicine by Kristian Axelsson and Mattias Lorentzon of the University of Gothenburg, Sweden, and colleagues.

mix_items.title: Next-generation RNA approach provides hope for genetic diseases missed by current drugs
mix_items.summary: Researchers at the University of Toronto have developed a next-generation RNA therapeutic approach with the potential to treat a wide range of genetic diseases that share certain disease-causing mutations. The work advances an emerging platform in genetic medicine centered on transfer RNA, or tRNA. The team engineered tRNA to help cells read through premature stop signals and complete production of full-length proteins that would otherwise be truncated or absent.

mix_items.title: Largest ever molecular map of autism opens new paths to precision therapies
mix_items.summary: For more than two decades, researchers have identified hundreds of genes that increase the risk of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). Yet multiple fundamental questions have remained unanswered: Among them, how do mutations in these genes lead directly to changes in brain development, and how can that knowledge be translated into more effective therapies?

mix_items.title: Students find AI isn't a cure all for drug discovery
mix_items.summary: There's been a lot of talk about artificial intelligence's potential to transform drug research and discovery—and companies are spending billions in pursuit of that dream.

mix_items.title: Chronic pain is reflected in the folds and grooves of the cerebral cortex
mix_items.summary: Persistent pain often has no clear cause. However, studies show measurable differences in the structure and activity of the brains of those affected. This might explain why they experience chronic pain. "Many of our study participants were grateful that someone was taking their symptoms seriously and conducting research into them," says neuroscientist Salome Häuselmann.

mix_items.title: Swimming in rivers and lakes linked to higher risk of stomach bugs and rashes
mix_items.summary: People swimming in rivers and lakes could be putting themselves at risk of nasty skin conditions and stomach bugs, according to a new study from the University of East Anglia. The researchers found that people who swam in rivers and lakes were more than twice as likely to develop skin problems, while higher levels of bacteria linked to fecal pollution were associated with an increased risk of stomach bugs.

mix_items.title: Tailoring the 'caffeine nap' to help drivers with obstructive sleep apnea manage tiredness behind the wheel
mix_items.summary: Researchers have issued tailored advice for drivers with obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) after finding that common guidance for tackling tiredness behind the wheel may not be the most effective approach for people with the condition.

mix_items.title: US environmental groups plan to sue to relist gray whales under Endangered Species Act
mix_items.summary: A group of environmental organizations announced their intent to sue the United States National Marine Fisheries Services (NMFS) for failing to consider protections for Eastern Pacific gray whales under the Endangered Species Act (ESA). Gray whales (Eschrichtius robustus) are experiencing a potentially catastrophic population decline, a sharp reversal from what had been considered a conservation […]

mix_items.title: JWST finds early galaxies may be 4 times more massive than thought
mix_items.summary: Astronomers using JWST have discovered that massive early galaxies contain far more small, faint stars than expected. That hidden population could make some of these galaxies three to four times more massive than previous estimates. The finding makes it even harder to explain how enormous, mature galaxies formed so soon after the Big Bang. It could also suggest that planets around low-mass stars were more common in the early universe than scientists realized.

mix_items.title: Archaeologists discover mysterious 400-year-old Indigenous pot in Florida
mix_items.summary: A tiny, fully intact Indigenous pot buried for roughly 400 years has left archaeologists wondering why such a usable object was deliberately abandoned. Found at a historic Potano-Timucua village in Florida, the mysterious vessel is helping reveal a complex world of Native traditions, Spanish influence, trade, and migration.

mix_items.title: 3,500-year-old skeletons challenge what scientists thought they knew about syphilis
mix_items.summary: Ancient remains from Vietnam suggest diseases like yaws may have been passed from mother to child thousands of years ago, a form of transmission often assumed to indicate syphilis. The discovery could overturn how scientists interpret ancient infections and complicate the long-running mystery of syphilis’s origins.

mix_items.title: Scientists find evidence for two origins of life on Earth
mix_items.summary: Scientists probing life’s deepest origins have uncovered evidence that the first free-living cells may have emerged not once, but twice. The findings suggest a striking possibility: life may share one ancient genetic code, yet have undergone two separate transitions into free-living existence.

mix_items.title: “Cannot be explained” – New super steel stuns scientists
mix_items.summary: Scientists have created an unusually corrosion-resistant stainless steel that could replace costly titanium components used to produce green hydrogen. The breakthrough could reduce structural material costs by roughly 40 times and make seawater-based hydrogen production far more economical.

mix_items.title: King Harold may have lost England by backing the wrong pope
mix_items.summary: A forgotten fragment of a lost papal letter is offering a surprising new explanation for the Norman Conquest. England may have backed the wrong pope during a bitter religious power struggle, giving Pope Alexander II a political reason to support William the Conqueror’s invasion. The discovery suggests Harold’s downfall in 1066 was shaped by intrigue in Rome as well as bloodshed at Hastings.

mix_items.title: 150-million-year-old dinosaur footprints reveal something strange about its walk
mix_items.summary: A spectacular 150-million-year-old trail of more than 130 footprints captures a giant sauropod making a complete loop before continuing on its way. Its uneven stride hints that the long-necked dinosaur may have been walking with a limp.

mix_items.title: The secret hidden in these ancient manuscripts isn’t written in ink
mix_items.summary: Researchers can now recover DNA from centuries-old parchment without damaging the manuscripts, turning historic documents into unexpected genetic time capsules. The hidden clues could reveal ancient trade routes, livestock history, manuscript origins, and details of everyday life stretching back more than a thousand years.

mix_items.title: Earth’s molten core suddenly reversed direction — and scientists don’t know why
mix_items.summary: Earth’s molten iron core unexpectedly reversed direction beneath the Pacific, revealing a dramatic change in the hidden engine that creates our planet’s magnetic field. Satellite data suggest the surge is already weakening, raising the possibility that the deep-Earth upheaval is part of a mysterious natural cycle.

mix_items.title: Scientists find unexpected life on Ötzi the Iceman’s 5,300-year-old body
mix_items.summary: More than 5,000 years after his death, Ötzi the Iceman is still hosting a remarkable mix of ancient and modern microorganisms. Researchers separated microbes that lived in his body during his lifetime from those that arrived after his death, uncovering traces of his original gut bacteria and cold-loving yeasts that may have survived alongside him in the glacier for millennia.

mix_items.title: Scientists rediscover lost Megalodon fossils—and reveal a 79-foot giant
mix_items.summary: Several enormous Megalodon vertebrae thought to have been destroyed in 1989 were found sitting unnoticed on a museum shelf. Their analysis strengthens evidence that the giant shark could exceed 24 meters (79 feet) in length and live for nearly a century. Researchers also estimate that its newborns may have measured an astonishing 3.6 meters (12 feet).
